title: Horseradish Cream
subtitle: Freshly grated root folded into double cream
excerpt: The proper companion to roast beef: fresh horseradish root grated and folded into whipped double cream with a little vinegar and mustard. Sharp, fiery, and completely different from the jarred version.

recipe.sourceNotes: Horseradish has been used as a condiment in Britain since at least the sixteenth century, when it appeared as a companion to beef and oily fish. The root contains allyl isothiocyanate, the same compound that gives mustard its heat, which is released when the root is grated and disperses quickly on cooking. This is why horseradish must be served raw: heat destroys the pungency. The combination of grated root with cream appears in Mrs Beeton and Jane Grigson and is the preferred form in traditional British cooking, as opposed to the vinegar-preserved cream-free sauce found in jars. Fresh horseradish root is available from good greengrocers and some supermarkets; wear gloves when grating as the vapours are strong.

content.text: Grate the horseradish root on the fine side of the grater and do this near an open window or away from the face: the volatile compounds are strong. Work quickly once grated as the pungency begins to fade on exposure to air. Do not whip the cream to stiff peaks; it should be softly whipped so it folds around the horseradish without becoming grainy.

items.preparation: fresh root, peeled and very finely grated

content.text: Whip the cream to soft peaks. Fold in the grated horseradish, vinegar, mustard, sugar, and salt. Taste and adjust: the sauce should be fiery, faintly sweet, and sharp. If using jarred prepared horseradish instead of fresh root, reduce the quantity to 2 to 3 tablespoons and taste before adding more.
Transfer to a bowl and refrigerate until needed. Best served within a few hours of making; the cream softens and the heat fades a little on standing. Serve cold alongside roast beef or smoked salmon.
